Those who violate international law must be held accountable, period. Other than that, we're not going to be able to move forward and address this challenge. Thank you, and thank you for having us here. Colombia's experience has taught us that respect for international humanitarian law is a legal obligation and helps preserve pathways towards peace. Its implementation reduces human suffering, protects essential services, and helps preserve the social fabric, as we have all mentioned here. But protecting civilians also requires legitimate state presence, the rule of law, and strong national and local capacities. Where institutions are weak or absent, civilians are more exposed to armed groups, forced displacement, recruitment, and other forms of violence. So peace must be grounded in accountability and concrete, verifiable commitments. We have found that dialogue alone cannot protect civilians if violence continues on the ground. Those who genuinely seek peace must translate commitments into action by ending violence against civilians, respecting international humanitarian law, and moving toward legality and accountability. Facilitating humanitarian access and clarifying the fate of missing persons can reduce suffering and support reconciliation. Third, we find that respect for international humanitarian law must be upheld by all parties to armed conflict. Protecting civilians, humanitarian personnel, and humanitarian operations is an obligation that cannot depend on political considerations. Finally, Colombia has learned that international cooperation is most effective when it strengthens national institutions and local capacities rather than replacing them. International partners, including OCHA, can support coordination, humanitarian access, and civilian protection while reinforcing the ability of states and communities to prevent, respond to, and recover from crisis. Through the Global Initiative to Galvanize Political Commitment to IHL, Colombia reaffirms its commitment to strengthening respect for IHL and protecting civilians worldwide. Thank you.

Thank you, Tom. I think -- Thank you, Tom. You hear me now? Okay. Yes. Thank you, Tom. Let me start by first of all thanking you personally for the reform, for this initiative, for the 87 million prioritization plan, which Saudi Arabia supports, and I'm glad that we are part of the picture that you have showed earlier, and so that we believe in both commitment, we believe in coordination, we believe in localization, we believe in access, prevention, all of it. But let me take you to my medicine, since you introduced me in medicine. I was taught in medicine when I was young -- and I'm still young, Tom -- that prevention is the way to cure mass population. You have to prevent an accident, a disease, obesity, smoking, you name it. And that's why the ministries of health in countries will invest in prevention. So I would probably say that the fairest definition is prevention. Now, after prevention, I think We will go to the plan, how to plan, which you have actually indicated very well, and then we prepare and proceed. But that's easier done, and that will take us from the four Ds to the four Ps: prevent, plan, prepare, and proceed, which is another addition to your four Ds. Now, going now in the action and implementation, I think the process with the limited resources becomes very challenging. Now with the existing many conflicts, now there is no access, violation, targeting, and you name it. And unless we prevent that and put a stop to it, and we have heard enough of this, I don't want to repeat it, that's not going to go. No, and then I'll take you to a story from the Rohingya camp back in 2018, I visited the camp. And actually, I went to one of the refugee camps, barely a camp, barely a shelter, nothing in it. And there was a woman, blind, with three children. So I asked her a question, ma'am, I'm coming from Saudi Arabia, what do you need? And she lifted her hand, and she said, I am the happiest person on earth. Look at her priority. I said, "Why?" She said, "My husband and two children were burned in front of me." So they were killed in front of her, and for her to escape and have three children left for her to support her is her priority number one. So that's where the human dignity is, and that's where our challenge is. If we don't protect a woman like this, then we are not doing well. Thank you.

Thank you, Dr. Oduye. Okay, Amy. I mean, it doesn't say this on my card, but a lot of humanitarian data is a complete mess. You've been thinking about how we sort this out across the ISC, but also across UNAT, and you've been leading a lot of the work on this. how do we sort out our data?

Okay, so first of all, it's all about the data, right? If you go into a humanitarian crisis, the humanitarian coordinator actually has no clear picture of what's happening, right? I've done disaster response in the United States. We always have a common operating picture where everybody feeds in and you know what's happening and you see who has capacity, you see where the problems are, and then the coordinator can figure out where do we allocate the resources that are needed. Right now, our humanitarian coordinators basically get an Excel sheet from one agency and maybe they'll get a bit of data from another one and they'll maybe get an anecdote from another. That's not a way to run a crisis response. Right? So number one, we need to find ways to bring our data together. And I think actually with AI, there are some good opportunities, even if our data is not completely interoperable now, to connect it so we have a common operating picture. Second, I actually think there are some opportunities that we can take advantage of. We'll need some investments. Take satellite imagery. Right now, satellite imagery can read a flow of people much faster than any human could do. It'll take us a week to read the imagery to understand what's happening. Satellites can tell us within hours, within minutes of where people are moving and where we need to put our resources. So getting that investment in that AI capacity, but then I'm going to put a little cautionary note here, because there are pretty big gaps in the way AI now works, right? It's great if you're an American or European, not so great if you live in Ethiopia, Sudan, Yemen, all the places we work. So we still need people, and we need our folks to bring their good judgment, but bring their judgment to a common data picture so that we can interpret it in the most effective, most efficient ways.

So, Ute, now this is one where I think a lot of humanitarians in the room will listen very carefully to the answer to this question, because we've talked a lot about how humanitarians need to reset, be more efficient, more effective, more prioritized. How can donors do a donor reset?

Thanks so much. Well, Well, first of all, I must say that I still trust that we are doing something in a right way anyway, so we will not change everything, but of course, of course, we also, we have to really get our forces together and see what we really prioritize. But let me say a few words on this defined issue, and of course, first of all, thank you so much for organizing this event, which is hugely important, and I hope that we... We all learned a lot tonight. So as Finland, we, of course, we firmly support the UN-coordinated humanitarian system and its unwavering dedication to save the lives of those most in need. And the humanitarian reset has focused a lot on efficiency. And as you said, so that keeps you awake and many others maybe as well. But we have no other option but to be more efficient. But we also must sharpen our focus on the quality of aid. So it is not only about the amount, but also the quality of aid on people in the most vulnerable situations. Dollars used per person assisted cannot be our only metric. But we must keep the principle of impartiality of needs-based assistance in mind. And we, as Finland, welcome very much the UN's longstanding investment in evidence-based decision making in humanitarian assistance. And through the reset, the focus on data, as we heard, operational realities, and analysis has even sharpened. So we also thank you for communicating about data openly. In planning and executing life saving assistance, it is also crucial to consider how assistance impacts those most vulnerable, such as persons with disability and gender equality. We welcome the decisions to allocate. funds from CERF to deliver life-saving services to women and girls and to disability inclusion. In addition to our core funding to CERF, Finland is preparing to allocate 2 million euros for disability inclusion, and we encourage also others to do so. Every human being's life-saving needs require more than shelter and food. Finland warmly supports that life-saving aid in the most severe humanitarian crisis also includes education to children. Attending school can give children a sense of normalcy in stressful and life-threatening situations. School meal programs help to ensure that children receive nutritious food. Education equips children with tools for everyday life, thus uplifting every child and contributing to more resilient and stable societies. And to conclude, Finland calls for a renewed commitment to upholding international humanitarian law and its faithful interpretation to reach those most in need. We all need to hold the line for principled humanitarian action. Thanks.

Thank you. So, Joaquin, I want to come to another of the most controversial aspects of what we're doing at the moment through the reset, which is this worry that we all have, and Alexandra articulated it earlier on, that that bridge from the humanitarian emergency response to development is fraying. And as we are forced to prioritize more towards lifesaving work, that we're not doing enough, therefore, to ensure that the early recovery, the resilience, and ultimately development is being set up in the right way. It's something, one of the many things that keeps me awake at night. How can we get better at doing this?

Thank you. Good afternoon. Well, I'm not Joaquin. Joaquin had to leave. Oh, sorry. Sorry, but I'm general director for Europe, so I'm updated with these issues, sadly, because I had to coordinate the European response due to the twin earthquakes in my country. So, yes, I am Well, first of all, very thankful on behalf of my country to OCHA and ECHO for all the help that we coordinated together. It was a swift response that demonstrated that humanitarian aid, in order to be effective, need to be timely and well-coordinated with the inside authorities. So of course, today, our challenges are constantly evolving. helping during the humanitarian crisis is not only, uh, respond, uh, quick, but, uh, after that comes rebuild, uh, and assist the affected population. In our, uh, case, we do have a huge challenge ahead, um, not only rebuilding, uh, houses. but rebuilding an entire city, and also providing the right social aid to the affected population. For us, recovery cannot mean leaving humanitarian needs behind. While homes and infrastructure are rebuilt, people must continue to have access to education, health, essential services, water, electricity, and in some, dignity. This require, of course, careful manage transition, preserving humanitarian assistance, while progressively strengthening recovery, reconstruction, resilience, and national capacities. Therefore, we believe strongly in international cooperation. We are continuing to rebuild the bridges with every country in the world. We are very, very grateful. We received aid from more than 20 countries in just 70 hours. We received almost 1,000 persons that arrived to our country in order to help. tons, hundreds of tons of humanitarian aid. So thank you again.

Thank you very much.

And perhaps to say something which will be very controversial, particularly to humanitarian fundraisers, but Venezuela is a great example now of one of the hyper-prioritized campaigns which is well-funded. Now, of course, we all want more funding for the needs that go beyond that immediate hyper-prioritized plan, but actually the ask right now is for development funding for Venezuela. If you're making a choice, that is where, and I may lose my job for saying this, direct it towards the development actors right now, because that's where the needs are. our greatest. Finally, on this table, DNA, we're coming to you. How do we get over this every year? We're going to be back here next year saying, we need to reach this number of million people. We have this much money. We're this much short. Please help us. How do we get past this sort of incremental approach to what we do?

We need more money. We need more money. We need money because people are dying. for all life-saving activities, they need to happen now. We need to stop pretending that health protection and dignity are two separate things. I think for me, that's absolutely critical. And in this time where there is lack of resources, that's absolutely critical for me. The second thing that is very critical, for women, they don't stop having babies because it's war or because it's conflict or because we have a earthquake, et cetera. They still continue to live. So it is important that those lifesaving activity and that continuum can happen. And to make a link with what Alexander said a little bit, the continuum for development is As well, people are the foundation of future generation. So some countries today suffer so much that their future generation are at risk because women cannot deliver in the safest place. So results are important. But my question, Tom, would be for all of us, what if the service we deliver today together were not existing? What would happen for any given country? Thank you.

Thank you, D&O. Thank you very much. And thank you to this table for some brilliant contributions there that really highlight the challenge of prioritization. And unless enormous amounts of money suddenly appears from nowhere, we're going to have to carry on making these incredibly tough decisions. And so we want to make sure we're working together to do that in a principled way and really getting to where the needs are greatest. Let me come on to another issue that's been difficult this year and we haven't always got right, which is devolve. How can we really ensure that we are walking the talk on shifting not just resources, but genuine power, Yanti, towards our front lines?

Over to you. So it's 2026, I think the Grand Bargain is precisely a decade behind us. And there were a couple of commitments we made in the Grand Bargain, particularly around localization and locally led. It was interesting to read the latest State of Humanitarian Systems report by ALNAP that came out only a few weeks ago. where it was very clear in what way there has been some delivery on the grand bargain, but also how, where, essentially, the pace has been glacial. And I think we can all agree that on localization in particular, we've seen that lack of pace and determination. The ALNAP report also calls out evidence-based interventions and modalities that have proven to work and be very effective and efficient. Let me call out a few. The use of cash as a modality, anticipatory action, so prevention to come back to the doctor here, prepositioning of stocks, very pragmatic and practical. building local capacity, and data and tech to come back to Amy's point around how do we use data tools. Now, what we see also is that although these things are evidence-based and have proven to work, they are more disinvested than other elements, particularly over the course of the last 18 to 24 months. So that is interesting observation. So the bits that seem to work best get less money. local capacity to call that out, and I will get to my friends here at the table. In the Grand Bargain, the Grand Bargain promise was 25% of funding. Now, that was just one element, one KPI to measure localization. That's not the whole thing, of course. It's also about power, responsibility, and resource allocation. But it is an indicator, 25%. In the ALNAP report, it stands at 4.3. This is shocking. you know, indication of the fact that we agree these things at summits and then we write big statements, but we don't actually do it. And this is man-made. So I'd love to hear from a couple of people here. We have Sami Khader, director of Man Development Center in OPT, a great longstanding operational agency on the ground and a great partner for Save as well. Sami, so what is the most frustrating obstacle to you to genuine locally led development and humanitarian action?

Thank you. Actually, let's go back to the word Humanitarian World Summit that was done in 2016. So 10 years passed, and still we are talking about localization. There is progress happened, but is it sufficient? I think it's not, till now. The figures shows that 25, and sometimes in Palestine, this last year, it reached 38 percent. 34%, and in '24 reached 38% between national and international NGOs. Actually, localization means, according to the definition, shifting resources, power, and decision-making authority from the international actors to the national ones. Is this happening? Until now, there are a lot of debate on this, and there are a lot of obstacles, actually, and I'll talk frankly about some of the obstacles from our experience for the last three decades in Palestine. First of all, the imbalance of power. There is imbalance of power between the national and international actors. There is not enough trust about this. The second important thing is that the risk transfer. There is no risk sharing. We are, as national NGOs, we are responsible for all the risks that comes from the external environment, from the occupation, from the killing, from the and all the confiscation of lands, confiscating our properties, and killing our people. As man, we lost 29 persons during this war in Gaza, 29 persons who were killed, and we should be responsible for all the risks that comes from the external. This is not fair. The third thing is the There is no capacity building component to develop the capacities of the NGOs. We need to develop the capacities. If you need a strong organization, you have to build their capacity, you have to build their systems to be able to deliver, uh, and, uh, services, quality services and accountable, uh, services to the people. Also, the competition. I have to mention that there is, till now, severe competition between the national organization and the international organization. Some international NGOs, and I think the majority of them, they believe that they should do the work as enabler and not implementing agencies. But we also face that many international NGOs, they are act acting to replace the Palestinian NGOs or the national NGOs or to compete with them. So we need to move from competition to complementarity role between the two players, the main players. And also, there is an issue here regarding the complexity of the compliance requirements in the HF. There are a lot of things to be asked by the national organization to fulfill. And this is an exhausting task that we have to fill and we have to fulfill every time that we have a new project, we have to do due diligence, we have to do micro assessment, we have to do spot check, and all these things. This will limit the participation and the engagement of the CBOs and the small NGOs. This is why you feel that you have few numbers of NGOs that are able to meet the requirements of this system. We need this system to be simplified. to be simplified so to give access and to give a space to the CPOs. And also, we have another issue that we feel that it's important to consider that there is, uh, that localization is still a ter- a terminology that is fake. Everybody is, uh, uh, defining this, uh, term in, at his own. So we need to define and we need to develop trackers, you know, how we can track the localization in numbers, in monitoring what is happening on the ground. The other thing that also we feel that there is resistance from some international NGOs especially during the war, during the last 1,083 days of suffering in Gaza. There are new NGOs, new NGOs that comes and they are working directly, implementing directly all the activities and competing on the same resources. So the competition is severe. And we have to cope with these things. The question, are the NGOs, the national NGOs able to lead? Yes, we are able to lead. And we are looking for a real equal partnership with international NGOs and not to replace anybody. We want your knowledge, your experience. We need to exchange information. And this is how we can build partnership. So we are looking for real partnership, and also the donors, we are asking the donors also not to have and to support short-term projects, six months, five months, and every time you have to run behind writing another proposal and going in the whole process. Let's talk about one year, two years, multi-year year projects that can serve. And also, I request from our UN agencies to have one unified process. So if you are asking the national NGOs to do due diligence, the results should be applied to all UN agencies, and not every time we have to go into this exercise. The same with micro assessment. The micro assessment takes a lot of time from the national NGOs. So I believe that building partnership, equal partnership, simplifying the system, giving space to the CBOs and other NGOs, I think in this we can meet the real requirements and the real needs of our people. Thank you.

That was a wonderful and practical, and surely it doesn't sound like rocket science either. Peter Lauren, the Hilton Foundation, one of the leading philanthropic supporters of humanitarian responses worldwide, has been for years. How do you see the role of local actors having evolved and evolving even more? What investments are most critical today to make sure those local organizations can actually lead sustainable responses tomorrow?

Thank you, Yanti. And the third part is, how can you all get involved? As Dr. Sami said, we're not there yet. All right? In the past decade since the World Humanitarian Summit, we've seen an increase in rhetoric about the involvement of local organizations and local leaders in humanitarian fora, but it has not shifted finances, nor the quality of available dollars. and has yet to bring about any significant change in power dynamics. 2024, only $49 million went to refugee-led organizations, according to research conducted by the Overseas Development Institute. That's a drop in the bucket compared to the $4.7 billion that went to UN refugee response in that year, let alone the $13 billion that we're talking about in this room. And when we talk about the refugee-led organizations that have been funded, the grants are small. The average size of a grant is about $35,000, compared to $320,000 to a UN organization doing similar work. In the United States, if we compared this to women's and men's pay for equal work, we would have a scandal. Things have not improved because of the recent changes in the humanitarian system, so that's where we are now. Why does this matter? Okay, first of all, we cannot afford to sideline refugee-led organizations. They play an essential role in the refugee response. They're first-line responders. They're trusted by their communities, and therefore they have access where others do not. They're providing services that they know match the real needs of people on the ground. From Kampala to Bogota, we at the Hilton Foundation have seen refugee-led organizations step in to fill gaps left by a scaled-back international system. Because when everyone else leaves, the refugee-led organizations are still there. They're doing this on shoestring budgets and with the help of volunteers. If we want to see the real promise of refugee-led organizations, long-lasting impact for refugees and host communities, we need to properly resource them. OK, third part, it's not so hard. We have tried to do this at the Hilton Foundation ourselves. We started from a basis in our international grant making in general of about 15% going to local organizations in 2019. Today, we're at 35%, and our refugee program is at 60%. And we did a whole of org reorganization for this and a collaboration. You can do it as well. If a small, relatively small foundation in California can do this, the UN humanitarian system can do it. If we really want to move the needle, there are three things that we recommend. First, multi-year flexible funds directly into the hands of refugee-led organizations intermediaries, not only from my peers in philanthropy, but from many government donors who have committed to localizing their funding. Budget and staffing cuts are no excuse. Rather, they make the situation more imperative, and they give you the deal you're looking for. Second, fix the plumbing. Okay, we need to invest in improving registration pathways and pull funding mechanisms so that money reaches refugee led organizations directly not through layers of subcontracts that pass on all the risks and none of the overhead coverage and the Hilton Foundation I'll go on record as saying we would be happy to underwrite the thinking of how you might do that so that we can help this move along. And third, moving refugee leaders from consultation to governance, onto boards and into strategy as co-designers of the response, not just recipients of the aid. And the bottom line is, the next decade of refugee response is going to be locally led, whether we fund it that way or not. The only question is whether refugee-led organizations are resourced to lead it well, driving towards real and lasting change for refugees and local communities around the world. Please join us.

Very good, Peter, from the not so small foundation, I think, in California. And I heard a deal on the table there because I heard the word underwrite. So maybe I will break the rules a little bit and pivot to one of the larger donors in the room, Melinda Bohannon for the Department of Development here, the UK, third largest donor in absolute terms. You've heard the obstacles, you've heard some of Peter's solutions, what they've actually done over the last years is actually really impressive. How can donors genuinely incentivize this power shift?

Thank you. And I can be brief because I very much agree with the two previous speakers. So I think from the donor perspective, or from actually it's the Foreign Office perspective, localization is very easy to say but really hard to do. It's very easy to say because the evidence is so clear that it is correct, it's more effective, it reaches local need more effectively, and there are organizations who have the capacity to channel the resources and to make a real difference. So why is it so hard to do? Well, the first reason is it takes a lot of time to build the relationships of trust and empower those relationships, and to convince and convince again politicians who are making decisions about resources that that's going to work. It involves giving up power, and everyone likes power. I challenge all of us in this room to think about that. I mean, it certainly has been for all of us in the UK a conscious choice about how to devolve it and when to devolve it and how. It does involve taking more risk if you're reporting to your MPs about where the money's gone and you're working through local systems that perhaps have less capacity than you're used to. And let's face it, it involves making very tough choices. Who knows who the most effective local actor is going to be on the ground? There are so many. And for what it's worth, I would include some international NGOs in that list. They are themselves often very localized. They have chosen to localize their offices and work through local power brokers. So easy to say, really hard to do. How does one go about it? I mean, I think the first thing is to recognize those challenges, to make long-term choices at country level about the partners that you work with to build their capacity over time, to trust them. It doesn't only have to be non-government organizations. It can be local research organizations, local universities, schools, hospitals. These are all relationships that you have to think about extremely carefully as you're thinking about your end goals in terms of what you're trying to finance and who you're trying to reach. Recently in the Nepal floods, for example, the reason we were able to switch our response so quickly, the 5 million pounds, was because we'd built up trusted relationships over time with local researchers, local NGOs, and local actors, and we could do it very quickly. Had we not been on the ground investing in those relationships, that would have been a lot harder. Other ways, I think there is a role for you and pooled funds. Tom, I know you've been championing this to really skip out or miss out rather the middleman or the middle person where we can so we can get to local actors. I think we all have a responsibility as the donor community to get behind you in that endeavor. That said, international agencies, also play a critical role and we have to understand and respect that, particularly where human rights law is under threat and humanitarian actors are under threat. And as I say, very often they themselves are localised. And the last thing I wanted to say is... I think we need to be really clear as a community that we are comfortable with a mixed approach. We have to understand what international organizations do. We have to work with our INGO partners. The NT represent a key partner for the UK government over many years. Thank you for that. But I think exactly the experience of MARN, and I've worked with MARN previously two decades ago, one of the most inspiring, I think, organizations on the ground in Palestine. There are many like that. It's finding them, it's working with them and it's investing in those relationships over time. It's person-to-person contact. It's not just a financial transaction.
Thank you. Very good.
I think over to-- Ms. Over to DNA.

Over to DNA. Thank you, Jhanti. 87 million lives delivering. That's the time. So how do we use radical transparency to reduce the cost of humanitarian action? It's about money to save lives. I'm going to start with Honorable Guevara Man from Panama. Where are you? Mucho gusto. Given Panama's unique experience as a regional humanitarian logistic hub, What additional measure could the international community and member state take to reduce delivery times and overcome bottleneck in the movement of humanitarian relief supply during emergency? Por favor.

Thank you very much. So as you said, as a logistics hub, we are committed to reducing response times and avoiding bottlenecks. So from our perspective, this requires stronger inter-institutional coordination simplified and digitalized customs procedures, and pre-agreed emergency protocols that can be activated immediately. Regular simulation exercises with UN agencies, national entities as well, can also help us identify delays and improve response times. Our goal in Panama and elsewhere for sure is to ensure that our strategic location translates into faster, more efficient, and more predictable humanitarian assistance throughout the region. Thank you.

Muchisima gracias, Excelentisimo. Kuwait, Honorable Sadik Marafi, Minister, Salaam. How can member state and humanitarian actors strengthen coordination and targeted diplomacy to secure safe and impeded humanitarian access, strengthen the protection of civilian, and better address humanitarian needs?

First of all, thank you very much for organizing this important discussion. Tom, thank you very much for your leadership and for your support, which we are in Kuwait fully in support to your work and duties. I think and I believe field trips is one of the important elements of receiving funds, supporting even people in need, but not any field trip. We have to create or start with a field trip that those who are in the field trip are, first of all, decision makers. Maybe I have raised this matter or this idea during the last donor group meeting of the ICRC in London in June, I think we have to have a level of ministers, even prime ministers, to be in the field, because connecting with those who are in need is very important. And then they will continue and go back and knows how those people are suffering. especially even in some fields that it's difficult to reach even. So this is an important element that we have to think about and work on.
Thank you. WFP, Carr, my dear Carr, how has the work on logistic and supply chain changed the sector, and what is next?

Great, thanks. And maybe I just say a few words on the context, because I think that's important on the why. I mean, we see record levels of global hunger now. It's driven by conflict. We have never seen more conflict since the Second World War. It's driven by now the disruptions to maritime trade with the three choke points in the Black Sea, the Strait of Hormuz, and now the Strait of Bab el-Mandeb. And it's driven by extreme weather events. We saw what happened in Nepal a couple of weeks ago, and we're really frightened about El Nino, the super El Nino that is coming at us. And this is all compounded by the lack of resources, but also the challenge to the respect of international humanitarian law, as was discussed earlier today. So, you know, certainly we will need more resources, more money, as you said, Jan. We also need, you know, member states to really step up on finding political solutions to these conflicts and protect humanitarian workers in these contexts. But, you know, it's also up to us as humanitarians. What can we do more to do better with less to squeeze out as much assistance as possible for every dollar that we manage to mobilize, to be as efficient and effective as possible. I mean, there are many ways, but one of the ways is this joint initiative around supply chains that we brought forward together with UNICEF. You know, 70% of the resources in the humanitarian sector is related to supply chains. So, you know, there are huge opportunities here. We have come together to have lead agencies around procurement to join up freight forwarding and warehousing and to have the best position to deliver on the last mile. This will really bring huge economies of scale, strengthen our ability to deliver, including in the hardest to reach places. We are now piloting this in five countries. We're building also, I should say, on the experience of UNHAS, the Humanitarian Air Service, which 20, 25 years ago, everyone were doing their own. Now it's one joined up service that does it for everyone. And we are piloting in five countries. We hope to have the results in the next few weeks. And the idea is to, before the end of the year, to scale this up in all the 25 humanitarian operations. So it's one example, but there are many, many more. And we are tapping every stone on our side and making sure that we're working together, focusing on joint outcomes. Thank you.

Tack, tack, tack. Delivering with radical transparency. Honorable Minister from Malta in the room, Chris Fern, not arrived, was supposed to arrive late. All right. So I'm passing to Google, Maggie Johnson. You represent two of the biggest and most influential technology company on earth. From the perspective of the private sector, what would radical transparency look like? How can data and artificial intelligence help us to deliver assistance faster and more efficiently to those in need?

Thank you. AI and data are really critical to crisis response and resilience. These are really important priorities for Google. Every year, billions and billions of alerts go out over Android, Google Search, Google Maps, warning people all over the world that hurricanes, floods, earthquakes are coming, and other natural disasters. this is, all of these systems function because of AI and data. So they're really critical for many of the things that we've been talking about here. Now, Google.org is Google's philanthropic organization. And we've also been really involved with anticipatory action, which is this idea of actually trying to be there ahead of time when a crisis occurs. So one of the things that we've done is we've supported the Humanitarian Data Exchange, which is HDX signals, which is a combination of both humanitarian and geographic data. And it's one of the most important early warning systems that we have. Using the information from this system and advanced AI forecasting tools, we really can get closer to the 87 million goal. One of the things that we are going to do is we're going to reinvest in the system with OSHA, and that's going to be about 1.7 million to scale the system. And with that, the funding will actually go to deploying new, you know, like really brand new flood and cyclone models that will be implemented in the system, as well as training OSHA staff to use it in really effective ways. This is going to reach 1.5 million people around the world. ahead of a natural disaster, and that's going to be in about 15 countries, and hopefully we'll save lives and livelihoods because of that. Thank you.
Thank you so, so very much. Microsoft, President, Justins Fellow. The same question from another angle.

Thank you. I really reflected on this question of radical transparency, and it made me feel guilty, and I am guilty of something. I've worked with IOM and UNICEF and Plan International and UNHCR and virtually every humanitarian organization in this room over the last decade to build the digital capabilities that run a lot of these organizations in partnership with my friends at Google. And what I've realized is we have done a phenomenal job building the systems that support organizations. but not the systems that always support the beneficiaries, the people that we're trying to support in the field.
